title: Idle hours
translation: Nothing to do all day, so I sit here with my ink and write down whatever drifts through my head, one useless thing after another, in no particular order. It's strange. Almost a kind of madness.
original: つれづれなるままに、{日|ひ}ぐらし{硯|すずり}に{向|むか}ひて、{心|こころ}に{移|うつ}り{行|ゆ}くよしなしごとを、そこはかとなく{書|か}きつくれば、{怪|あや}しうこそ{物狂|ものぐる}ほしけれ。
literal: Having nothing to do, facing the inkstone all day long, as I write down, without any order, the trivial things that pass through my mind, it is strangely, madly (feeling).

notes.text: つれづれ: long empty hours with nothing to do, often with a feeling of tedium. The book takes its name from these first words: 徒然草 is read つれづれぐさ, and 徒然 is a kanji spelling of つれづれ.
'All day long', from {日|ひ} 'day' and {暮|く}らす 'to spend (time)'.

よし 'reason, point' + なし 'there is none' + こと 'things'. So the author calls his own book 'pointless stuff' in the first sentence. It is a humble opening, and it is also the 1330 version of 'random thoughts, nothing serious'.
'Without any clear order', 'just as it comes'. The book really is like this: 243 sections, from death and Buddhism to court etiquette and a priest with a pot on his head (section 53).

notes.quote: 怪しうこそ物狂ほしけれ
notes.text: こそ … けれ: こそ gives emphasis, and the sentence must then end in the realis form ({已然形|いぜんけい}): {物狂|ものぐる}ほし becomes {物狂|ものぐる}ほしけれ. This pattern is {係|かか}り{結|むす}び. {怪|あや}しう is {怪|あや}しく with a sound change (ウ{音便|おんびん}). Scholars do not agree on who is 'mad' here: the writer, who feels strange, or the writing, which turns out strange. The translation keeps it open.
